decline: Killed by strategic drift, not by failure: 19M users (2011), 70-minute average sessions, 230 games and 8,000+ virtual items in its marketplace — but the PS4 generation had 'no plans' for it and Sony would not port it. A third place with no org chart to live in. Purchased virtual goods died with the servers; TechTudo reports no refunds for bought items.
levi_application: core/levi/games/parlor.py (built this wave): the parlor is a third place with nothing to purchase and therefore nothing to revoke. Handles, bulletin posts, and game-night records are plain JSON under ~/.levi/games/parlor/ — the player owns the building, not a tenancy.
mechanism: The first mainstream persistent avatar lobby on a console: customizable avatars, private spaces decorated with earned trophies, public minigames (bowling alley, arcade cabinets), branded event rooms (a Ghostbusters firehouse meetup, virtual E3 booths). It proved a console third place could hold 70-minute sessions — presence, not content, was the draw.

provenance.notes: Dates and figures verified against GamesIndustry.biz, TechSpot, and The Escapist shutdown reporting. 'No refunds' per TechTudo reporting.

revival_recipe: Keep the place; drop the landlord. A local-first lobby needs none of Sony's infrastructure: presence is a handle list, decoration is data the player owns, events are scheduled sessions. The revival is ownership inversion — the parlor exists on the player's machine, so no 'shifting landscape' can evict it.
skepticism: The 'rife with bugs / difficult to police' reading comes from a user forum retrospective, not Sony; Sony's stated reason was only 'a shifting landscape'. Profitability claims for Home are anecdotal.
summary: Sony's persistent 3D social world for PS3 (public beta Dec 2008): avatars, private trophy-decorated spaces, public minigames, branded event rooms. Sony stopped new content Nov 12, 2014 and shut it down March 31, 2015 citing a 'shifting landscape' — no PS4 port, and players lost purchased virtual goods without refunds.
title: PlayStation Home (2008-2015): the evicted tenant class — a third place with no org chart

decline: Killed by engagement-velocity loss: Nintendo's own FAQ says users were 'shifting to social networking services' — the slow, moderated, wholesome network could not compete with Facebook/Twitter's velocity. Nintendo had 'no plans to implement any services to replace Miiverse'; the Switch outsourced social to Twitter/Facebook share buttons. The third place lost to the feed.
levi_application: The parlor's bulletin board is the Miiverse inversion: no review queue, no engagement ranking, no cross-game global reach — just a local board where posts appear in order, newest last, and the owner can delete. Small and local IS the moderation model. No one needs to outrun a feed when there is no feed.
mechanism: Positivity by design: every post passed a human moderation queue before appearing ('please wait'), which made Miiverse arguably the only wholesome major social network — and the only slow one. Game-tied community pages embedded the social layer inside the games themselves (Mario Maker level comments, Splatoon plaza posts, the Smash Miiverse stage). 112 titles lost in-game features when it died.

provenance.notes: Verified against GamesIndustry.biz, Delisted Games, and Nintendo's official FAQ as quoted by NintendoEverything.

revival_recipe: Shrink the blast radius to the household. The wholesome-by-moderation trick worked because the community was small relative to the moderation; a local board with a dozen players needs no queue at all. Embed the board in the games (like Miiverse embedded in titles) but keep the data local and portable.
skepticism: GamesIndustry.biz notes Miiverse's closure reasons were 'largely of Nintendo's own making' (no links to outside social networks); the 'shifting to social networks' framing is Nintendo's own PR and should be read skeptically.
summary: Nintendo's social network built into Wii U/3DS games (launched 2012): game-tied community pages, handwritten posts, human-moderated review queues. Shut down Nov 7, 2017 because 'many users are shifting to social networking services'; 112 titles lost in-game social features. Players could download their own posts but not comments — the graph died with the servers.
title: Miiverse (2012-2017): the only wholesome network, outrun by the feed

decline: Killed by monetization refocus: Disney shuttered the browser original March 30, 2017 to force players onto the mobile reboot Club Penguin Island, whose in-app purchases and advertising were 'perceived as a betrayal of the original game's principles' and which could not carry progress or items over. Island itself died Dec 20, 2018 — Disney HR cited 'global competition' — with the entire Kelowna team laid off three weeks after being greenlit for two more years. The surviving fan remakes are noted for lacking the moderation that made the original a haven.
levi_application: The parlor encodes the Club Penguin lesson as law: safety is a property of scale and ownership, not of a trust-and-safety budget. The parlor holds a household's players; there is no stranger graph to moderate, no ad inventory to sell, no reboot to force-migrate toward. The charter's default-honest manifests (no paid randomness, no FOMO timers, hints free) are the anti-Island rules.
mechanism: The safe third place as product: a kid-safe MMO whose real infrastructure was a moderation operation parents trusted — minigames, parties, and puffles on top, trust underneath. It proved a third place could be deliberately small, safe, and profitable without engagement-maxing.

provenance.notes: Dates verified against Wikipedia (Club Penguin Island); Island shutdown/layoff details per the Kotaku-obtained Disney Canada letter as reported on Wikipedia; reboot-critique analysis per hulkapps retrospective (secondary source, treat framing cautiously).

revival_recipe: Rebuild the haven, not the game: a persistent kid-safe hangout where the moderation budget is replaced by smallness — invitation-only handles, a local board, scheduled game nights with known players. The load-bearing part was never the minigames; it was the trust.
skepticism: The 'betrayal of principles' framing is from a secondary retrospective (hulkapps), not player surveys; exact revenue-vs-cost drivers for the closure are not public.
summary: The kid-safe virtual world (2005-2017): minigames, parties, puffles, and — the real product — a moderation operation parents trusted. Disney killed the browser original March 30, 2017 to push the mobile reboot Club Penguin Island, whose in-app purchases alienated the core; Island was killed Dec 20, 2018 and the whole team laid off.
title: Club Penguin (2005-2017): the safe haven killed by its own reboot

decline: Killed by acquisition pivot: after buying the ailing platform in 2017, Microsoft shut it down March 10, 2023 amid 10,000 layoffs to 'focus our VR efforts on workplace experiences' via Mesh — cutting the entire AltspaceVR team. The consumer community was never the asset; the enterprise pivot was. The 2017 'rescue' reads in hindsight as a six-year talent-and-tech harvest.
levi_application: The parlor is acquisition-proof by construction: there is nothing to acquire — no company, no servers, no user graph, no IP beyond the player's own data. A third place that lives in ~/.levi/games/parlor/ cannot be pivoted to enterprise because there is no enterprise to pivot it to. This is the sunset-escrow principle (arch-games-sunset-crew) extended to social space: the funeral plan is that there is no funeral.
mechanism: The sly-generosity trade in pure form: a dying social-VR startup announces shutdown (summer 2017); the giant swoops in and 'saves' it; six years later the giant kills it anyway, harvesting the team and tech for its enterprise product. The community got six borrowed years and a download-your-data notice.

provenance.notes: Dates and layoff context verified against Engadget, The Register, and Road to VR; the 'harvest' reading is analysis, flagged as such.

revival_recipe: Make the third place un-acquirable: local-first data, open formats, no central account system. If a giant cannot buy the graph, it cannot pivot the graph. The revival recipe is the parlor's whole design — a place owned by the people in it.
skepticism: Microsoft's stated reason (Mesh workplace focus) is official; the 'talent harvest' reading is my analysis, not an insider claim. Road to VR confirms the 2017 rescue and 2023 kill timeline.
summary: Social VR platform (launched May 2015); ran out of money in 2017, was bought by Microsoft — then shut down March 10, 2023 so Microsoft could pivot VR to enterprise Mesh, cutting the entire AltspaceVR team. The community was inventory: saved for the team, killed for the roadmap.
title: AltspaceVR (2015-2023): saved by the giant, killed by the giant
